Inventory and Assortment Optimization under General Choice: A Unified Approximation Framework

Jacob Feldman    Yukai Huang    Heng Zhang
Abstract

We study joint inventory and assortment optimization under general substitutable choice models. Before a selling horizon, a decision maker selects initial product inventories subject to a capacity constraint on the total number of units stocked. Customers subsequently arrive sequentially and choose among the products offered to them. We consider two operating settings: show-all inventory selection, in which every in-stock product must be offered, and dynamic assortment personalization, in which the decision maker observes each customer’s type and may adapt the offered assortment to the remaining inventory and purchase history.

We develop a unified approximation framework that connects each operating setting to its corresponding static optimization problem. For show-all inventory selection, a polynomial-time α\alpha-approximation for cardinality-constrained static assortment optimization yields guarantees of 0.486​α0.486\alpha when the number of arrivals is deterministic or Poisson distributed and 0.4328​α0.4328\alpha when it follows an increasing-failure-rate (IFR) distribution. For personalization, the same guarantees hold when α\alpha instead denotes the approximation factor for joint assortment and customization, the static problem studied by El Housni and Topaloglu: selecting a common product catalog subject to a cardinality constraint and a customized assortment from that catalog for each customer type. Our approach combines a fluid relaxation, demand-dependent fractional inventory allocations, bounds on expected truncated demand, and dependent rounding. Notably, our personalized policy fixes one assortment for each customer type before the selling horizon and subsequently offers every in-stock product within that assortment. Thus, it requires no dynamic assortment reoptimization, despite competing against the optimal fully adaptive policy.

Finally, we construct instances in which optimal show-all revenue approaches only one-half of the fluid bound under deterministic arrivals and 1−w≈0.43285671-w\approx 0.4328567 under IFR arrivals, where w​ew=1we^{w}=1. With an exact static assortment oracle, our IFR guarantee can approach the latter factor arbitrarily

1 Introduction

A fundamental problem in retail operations is to determine which products to carry and how much inventory to stock before a selling season. These decisions are particularly challenging when customers substitute following stockouts: the demand for a product depends on the availability of other products, and hence on their initial inventory levels and realized sales. We consider two versions of this problem, both subject to a capacity constraint on the total number of units initially stocked. In the show-all (SA) setting, every in-stock product is offered to each arriving customer, so the assortment evolves only through stockouts. In the dynamic assortment personalization (DAP) setting, the decision maker observes each customer’s type and can offer a customized subset of the in-stock products. The latter provides additional flexibility but requires coordinating a common initial inventory across customers with heterogeneous preferences.

We develop a unified approximation framework for both problems under general substitutable choice models. Our approach separates the computational difficulty of selecting products from the stochastic difficulty of allocating inventory and managing stockouts. For SA, the relevant static optimization problem is cardinality-constrained assortment optimization. For DAP, it is joint assortment and customization (JAC): selecting a common catalog of at most BB products and an assortment from that catalog for each customer type. An approximation algorithm for the appropriate static problem serves as an oracle for a fluid relaxation, whose solution is converted into a feasible integral inventory decision through demand-dependent fractional allocations and randomized rounding. Importantly, our DAP policy fixes an assortment for each customer type before the selling horizon and subsequently offers every in-stock product from that assortment whenever the corresponding type arrives. Thus, although the benchmark permits fully adaptive assortment decisions, our policy requires no dynamic assortment reoptimization: assortments change only as their constituent products stock out. This illustrates how appropriately coordinated initial inventory and assortment decisions can substantially reduce the need for dynamic assortment control.

Related work on show-all inventory selection.

Early approximation algorithms exploit structure in customer preferences. Goyal et al. (2016) develop approximation schemes for structured preference lists, and Segev (2019) gives a quasi-polynomial-time approximation scheme for nested preferences. For general rank-based choice, Aouad et al. (2019) obtain revenue-dependent guarantees and a constant factor under uniform product revenues. Goldstein Feder and Segev (2023) improve this horizontally differentiated case and develop a universal inventory construction across arrival-count distributions. Under multinomial-logit (MNL) choice, Aouad et al. (2018) establish a constant-factor guarantee for increasing-failure-rate (IFR) arrivals, and Aouad and Segev (2023) develop an approximation scheme whose running time depends on the range of preference weights. More recently, Sun et al. (2025) provide SA guarantees of 0.474−ε0.474-\varepsilon for deterministic arrivals and 0.286−ε0.286-\varepsilon for IFR arrivals using MNL-specific structure.

Moving beyond specific parametric choice models, Fu et al. (2026) introduce a black-box reduction from cardinality-constrained assortment optimization to show-all inventory selection. Given an αSA\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}-approximation for the static assortment problem, their guarantees are approximately 0.272​αSA0.272\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}} for deterministic or Poisson arrivals and 0.25​αSA0.25\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}} for IFR arrivals. We retain their general substitutability assumption while improving these guarantees to 0.486​αSA0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}} and 0.4328​αSA0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}, respectively. Our analysis also gives matching or nearly matching examples for the gap between the stochastic optimum and the fluid relaxation: a factor of 1/21/2 for deterministic arrivals and the sharp factor 1−w≈0.43285671-w\approx 0.4328567 for IFR arrivals, where w​ew=1we^{w}=1.

Table 1 summarizes the SA comparisons alongside the static assortment oracles used to instantiate our guarantees. For MNL, cardinality-constrained assortment optimization is polynomially solvable, so αSA=1\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}=1 (Rusmevichientong et al. 2010). For rank-based choice with uniform product revenues, purchase probability is a weighted coverage function, and greedy optimization gives αSA=1−1/e\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}=1-1/e (Aouad et al. 2019). The latter guarantee continues to apply to the common price-adjusted rewards in our fluid separation problem. Our factors therefore specialize to 0.4860.486 and 0.43280.4328 for MNL and to approximately 0.30720.3072 and 0.27360.2736 for uniform-revenue rank-based choice, under deterministic/Poisson and IFR arrivals, respectively.

Related work on assortment personalization.

For DAP, Bai et al. (2025) study coordinated inventory stocking and assortment customization, providing constant-factor guarantees under MNL choice. Sun et al. (2025) subsequently improve these guarantees to 12​(1−1/e)−ε\frac{1}{2}(1-1/e)-\varepsilon for deterministic arrivals and 1/4−ε1/4-\varepsilon for arbitrary arrival-count distributions. Our approach differs in two important respects. First, we consider general substitutable choice models, reducing the computational component to the joint assortment and customization (JAC) problem. Second, and more importantly, our algorithm does not dynamically optimize assortments during the selling horizon. Instead, it selects the initial inventory and a fixed assortment for each customer type, subsequently offering all products from that assortment that remain in stock. Despite this restriction, we obtain approximation guarantees of 0.486​αJAC0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for deterministic or Poisson arrivals and 0.4328​αJAC0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for IFR arrivals, measured against the optimal fully adaptive DAP policy. For MNL choice, Udwani (2025) provide a JAC approximation arbitrarily close to 1/21/2, yielding guarantees approaching 0.2430.243 and 0.21640.2164, respectively. Although these constants do not improve the specialized MNL guarantees of Sun et al. (2025), our results show that simple type-specific show-all policies, combined with appropriately selected initial inventories, achieve provable performance guarantees even when compared with policies that continually adapt their assortments to the evolving inventory state.

1.1 Contributions

A unified static-to-dynamic approximation framework.

For both SA and DAP, we formulate a two-constraint fluid relaxation that separates static product selection from stochastic inventory implementation. Its columns are assortments for SA and customized assortment configurations with a common catalog for DAP. An approximate static oracle yields a solution supported on at most two columns. We construct a feasible fractional inventory for each supporting column and evaluate it using a separable lower bound on expected truncated demand. Dependent rounding (Gandhi et al. 2006) preserves this bound in expectation, because expected truncated demand is affine between adjacent integer inventory levels. The analysis does not require the stochastic revenue function to be concave or submodular.

Improved show-all guarantees and sharp fluid comparisons.

For an αSA\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}-approximation to cardinality-constrained assortment optimization, we obtain guarantees of 0.486​αSA0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}} for deterministic/Poisson arrivals and 0.4328​αSA0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}} for IFR arrivals. The deterministic/Poisson analysis uses a Poisson truncated-demand surrogate and a sharper conditional Cauchy–Schwarz bound. The IFR analysis replaces it with a geometric surrogate and optimally balances the two fluid constraints. With an exact oracle, the IFR factor can be made arbitrarily close to 1−w≈0.43285671-w\approx 0.4328567, where w​ew=1we^{w}=1; a matching instance makes this the sharp uniform factor relative to the fluid LP. A two-product MNL instance gives a corresponding upper limit of 1/21/2 on the fluid comparison for deterministic arrivals. These limits concern the relaxation, not approximation hardness relative to the stochastic optimum.

Personalization without dynamic assortment reoptimization.

We extend our framework to DAP through a configuration-based fluid relaxation that jointly selects initial inventory and an assortment for each customer type. An αJAC\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}-approximation for JAC yields guarantees of 0.486​αJAC0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for deterministic or Poisson arrivals and 0.4328​αJAC0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for IFR arrivals. A notable feature of our algorithm is its simplicity: after the initial planning stage, it implements a type-specific show-all policy, offering every available product from a predetermined assortment for each arriving customer type. In particular, the algorithm never strategically removes an in-stock product or reoptimizes assortments in response to stockouts. Nevertheless, its performance guarantees hold relative to the optimal adaptive DAP policy, which may modify assortments based on customer types, remaining inventory, and the entire purchase history. Our results therefore demonstrate that joint optimization of initial inventory and type-specific assortments can recover a substantial guaranteed fraction of the benefits of fully dynamic assortment optimization, without requiring dynamic assortment decisions.

2 Problem Formulation and Main Results

We study the joint optimization of initial inventory and assortment decisions under general customer choice models. The decision process unfolds in two stages. First, the decision maker (DM) selects the initial inventory levels of a collection of products, subject to a capacity constraint. Subsequently, customers arrive sequentially and make purchase decisions from the assortments offered to them. We consider two operating settings: show-all (SA) inventory selection, in which every in-stock product must be offered to each customer, and dynamic assortment personalization (DAP), in which the DM observes the arriving customer’s type and may customize the assortment offered from the available inventory. We first introduce the notation and assumptions shared by both settings, then formalize each problem and state our main approximation results.

2.1 Preliminaries

Products and customer choice.

Let 𝒩={1,…,n}\mathcal{N}=\{1,\ldots,n\} denote the collection of products, where each unit of product i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N} generates revenue ri≥0r_{i}\geq 0 when purchased. The no-purchase option is indexed by 00, with r0=0r_{0}=0.

Customers make purchase decisions according to a general discrete choice model. For any assortment S⊆𝒩S\subseteq\mathcal{N}, let π⁡(i,S)\pi(i,S) denote the probability that a customer purchases product ii when offered SS. We set π⁡(i,S)=0\pi(i,S)=0 for i∉Si\notin S and define π⁡(0,S)=1−∑i∈Sπ⁡(i,S)\pi(0,S)=1-\sum_{i\in S}\pi(i,S) as the no-purchase probability. In the personalized setting, customers belong to types k∈[K]k\in[K], each characterized by potentially different choice probabilities πk​(i,S)\pi^{k}(i,S). We use π⁡(i,S)\pi(i,S) when the choice model is common to all customers, as in the SA setting, and πk​(i,S)\pi^{k}(i,S) when distinguishing customer types is necessary. Choice probabilities are stationary within each type, and customer purchase decisions are independent across arrivals, conditional on the offered assortments and customer types.

We impose the following standard substitutability assumption, which requires that removing products from an assortment cannot decrease the purchase probability of a product that remains available.

{assumption}

[Substitutability] For any assortments A⊆S⊆𝒩A\subseteq S\subseteq\mathcal{N} and product i∈Ai\in A, we have π⁡(i,A)≥π⁡(i,S)\pi(i,A)\geq\pi(i,S). In the personalized setting, the same condition holds for every customer type k∈[K]k\in[K], i.e., πk​(i,A)≥πk​(i,S)\pi^{k}(i,A)\geq\pi^{k}(i,S).

This assumption is satisfied by a broad class of choice models, including MNL, mixed-MNL, and ranking-based models. Importantly, we do not impose any particular parametric structure on the choice probabilities.

Inventory and customer arrivals.

Before the selling horizon begins, the DM selects an initial inventory vector 𝒄=(ci)i∈𝒩\boldsymbol{c}=(c_{i})_{i\in\mathcal{N}}, where ci∈ℤ+c_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} denotes the number of units stocked for product ii. The total number of units stocked cannot exceed an integer capacity B≥1B\geq 1. Thus, the set of feasible initial inventory vectors is

𝒞B={𝒄∈ℤ+n:∑i∈𝒩ci≤B}.\mathcal{C}_{B}=\left\{\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}^{n}:\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}}c_{i}\leq B\right\}.

Inventory cannot be replenished during the selling horizon, and each purchase permanently consumes one unit of the corresponding product.

Let TT denote the total number of customer arrivals, with τ=𝔼⁡[T]\tau=\mathbb{E}[T]. We consider three arrival settings: (i) TT is a known deterministic integer; (ii) TT is Poisson distributed with known mean τ\tau; or (iii) TT follows a nonnegative integer-valued increasing-failure-rate (IFR) distribution with finite mean τ\tau. In the latter two settings, the realization of TT is not known to the DM in advance. The arrival count is independent of customer preferences. Additional assumptions concerning the distribution of customer types in DAP are introduced in Section 2.3.

Customers are indexed by t∈[T]t\in[T]. Let 𝒄t\boldsymbol{c}_{t} denote the remaining inventory immediately before customer tt arrives, with 𝒄1=𝒄\boldsymbol{c}_{1}=\boldsymbol{c}. In either operating setting, the DM offers an assortment St⊆{i∈𝒩:ci,t>0}S_{t}\subseteq\{i\in\mathcal{N}:c_{i,t}>0\}, and the customer selects an option jt∈St∪{0}j_{t}\in S_{t}\cup\{0\}. Inventory then evolves according to ci,t+1=ci,t−𝟏{jt=i}c_{i,t+1}=c_{i,t}-\mathbf{1}\{j_{t}=i\} for every i∈𝒩i\in\mathcal{N}.

For any fixed initial inventory and admissible assortment policy, expected revenue is obtained by taking the expectation of ∑t=1Trjt\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{j_{t}} over customer arrivals, types, and purchase decisions. We distinguish the two operating settings below.

2.2 Show-All Inventory Selection

Problem formulation.

In the show-all (SA) setting, the DM offers every in-stock product to each arriving customer. Thus, the assortment offered in period tt is St={i∈𝒩:ci,t>0}.S_{t}=\{i\in\mathcal{N}:c_{i,t}>0\}. The DM makes no assortment decisions during the selling horizon; the displayed assortment evolves endogenously as products stock out. In particular, the offered assortments form a nested sequence.

For a given initial inventory vector 𝒄\boldsymbol{c}, let Rev⁡(𝒄)=𝔼⁡[∑t=1Trjt]\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{c})={\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{j_{t}}] denote the expected revenue generated under the show-all policy. The dependence of jtj_{t} on the initial inventory vector is suppressed to simplify notation. The SA inventory selection problem is

OPTSA=max𝒄∈𝒞B⁡Rev⁡(𝒄).\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}=\max_{\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathcal{C}_{B}}\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{c}). (OPT-SA)

Computational assumption.

Our approach relies on the cardinality-constrained assortment optimization problem. For any reward vector 𝝆∈ℚn\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}, define

AOB(𝝆)=maxS⊆𝒩:|S|≤B∑i∈Sρiπ(i,S).\operatorname{AO}_{B}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq\mathcal{N}:\\ |S|\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in S}\rho_{i}\pi(i,S). (1)

We assume access to an algorithm that approximates this problem within factor αSA∈(0,1]\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}\in(0,1] in polynomial time, for any modified reward vector. The exact-oracle case corresponds to αSA=1\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}=1.

The role of this oracle is to solve a fluid relaxation of (OPT-SA) through dual separation. We denote the optimal value of this relaxation, introduced in Section 3.1, by OPTFL\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}. As established by Fu et al. (2026), OPTFL≥OPTSA\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}.

Deterministic and Poisson arrivals.

Our first result substantially improves the approximation guarantee obtainable from this relaxation when the number of customers is deterministic or Poisson distributed.

Theorem 2.1 (Deterministic and Poisson arrivals)

Suppose Assumption 2.1 holds and TT is either deterministic or Poisson distributed. If (1) can be solved optimally in polynomial time, then there exists a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that selects an integral inventory vector 𝐜^∈𝒞B\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}\in\mathcal{C}_{B} almost surely and satisfies

𝔼ω​[Rev⁡(𝒄^​(ω))]≥0.486​OPTFL≥0.486​OPTSA.\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathrm{Rev}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega))\right]\geq 0.486\,\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq 0.486\,\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}.

Here, ω\omega denotes the initial-inventory rounding randomness.

When only an αSA\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}-approximation for (1) is available, the guarantee becomes 0.486​αSA0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}, with an arbitrarily small additional loss that can be absorbed into the stated numerical constant.

The analysis also establishes that this guarantee is nearly tight relative to the fluid relaxation. In particular, we construct a sequence of MNL instances with deterministic arrivals for which OPTSA/OPTFL→1/2.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}/\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\rightarrow 1/2. Thus, no algorithm can guarantee a factor strictly larger than 1/21/2 relative to this fluid benchmark on all deterministic-arrival instances. Our 0.4860.486 guarantee is therefore close to the strongest possible factor obtainable through a direct comparison with this relaxation.

IFR arrivals.

We next consider the more general setting in which TT follows an IFR distribution. The main difficulty is that hypothetical product demand need not be dominated in convex order by a Poisson random variable with the same mean. We overcome this difficulty through a geometric-demand comparison and a modified inventory allocation, obtaining the following result.

Theorem 2.2 (IFR arrivals)

Suppose Assumption 2.1 holds and TT is a nonnegative integer-valued IFR random variable with finite mean. If (1) can be solved optimally in polynomial time, then there exists a randomized algorithm with expected polynomial running time that selects an integral inventory vector 𝐜^∈𝒞B\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}\in\mathcal{C}_{B} almost surely and satisfies

𝔼ω​[Rev⁡(𝒄^​(ω))]≥0.4328​OPTFL≥0.4328​OPTSA.\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathrm{Rev}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega))\right]\geq 0.4328\,\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq 0.4328\,\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}.

Moreover, the factor can be made arbitrarily close to γIFR=1−w≈0.4328567\gamma_{\mathrm{IFR}}=1-w\approx 0.4328567, where w∈(0,1)w\in(0,1) is the unique solution to w​ew=1we^{w}=1.

With an αSA\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}-approximation for (1), the guarantee becomes 0.4328​αSA0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}, again allowing an arbitrarily small additional computational loss.

The IFR guarantee is essentially tight relative to the fluid relaxation. We construct a sequence of instances with geometric arrival counts and substitutable choice probabilities for which

OPTSAOPTFL⟶γIFR.\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}}\longrightarrow\gamma_{\mathrm{IFR}}.

Together with Theorem 2.2, this shows that γIFR\gamma_{\mathrm{IFR}} is the sharp uniform comparison factor for the fluid relaxation under IFR arrivals.

These results apply to a broad class of substitutable choice models. For example, cardinality-constrained assortment optimization is polynomially solvable under MNL choice, giving αSA=1\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}=1. Under general ranking-based choice with uniform revenues, the greedy algorithm achieves αSA=1−1/e\alpha_{\mathrm{SA}}=1-1/e. Thus, the corresponding guarantees are 0.4860.486 and 0.43280.4328 for MNL, and approximately 0.30720.3072 and 0.27360.2736 for uniform-revenue ranking-based choice, under deterministic/Poisson and IFR arrivals, respectively.

2.3 Dynamic Assortment Personalization

Problem formulation.

We next consider the dynamic assortment personalization (DAP) problem. In this setting, customers belong to KK observable types, indexed by k∈[K]k\in[K], and a type-kk customer makes purchase decisions according to πk​(i,S)\pi^{k}(i,S).

When TT is deterministic, the customer arriving in period tt has type kk with probability λk​t\lambda_{kt}, where these probabilities may vary across periods. When TT is Poisson or IFR distributed, customer types are independent and identically distributed with probabilities λk\lambda_{k}, independently of TT. Customer types and preference realizations are independent across arrivals.

After observing the arriving customer’s type, the DM may offer any subset of the currently in-stock products. Moreover, the assortment decision may depend on the entire preceding purchase history and the remaining inventory vector. Thus, unlike SA, the DM may strategically withhold products that remain available and dynamically modify assortments as inventory is depleted.

Let ΣDAP​(𝒄)\Sigma_{\mathrm{DAP}}(\boldsymbol{c}) denote the collection of admissible nonanticipative personalized assortment policies under initial inventory 𝒄\boldsymbol{c}. For σ∈ΣDAP​(𝒄)\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{DAP}}(\boldsymbol{c}), let RevDAP​(𝒄,σ)=𝔼⁡[∑t=1Trjt]\mathrm{Rev}^{\mathrm{DAP}}(\boldsymbol{c},\sigma)={\mathbb{E}}[\sum_{t=1}^{T}r_{j_{t}}] denote the expected revenue under policy σ\sigma, where the expectation includes customer arrivals, types, purchase decisions, and any policy randomization. The DAP problem is

OPTDAP=max⁡supσ∈ΣDAP​(𝒄)𝒄∈𝒞B⁡RevDAP​(𝒄,σ).\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}=\max_{\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathcal{C}_{B}}\sup_{\sigma\in\Sigma_{\mathrm{DAP}}(\boldsymbol{c})}\mathrm{Rev}^{\mathrm{DAP}}(\boldsymbol{c},\sigma). (OPT-DAP)

Joint assortment and customization.

Our approach to DAP relies on a static optimization problem that jointly selects a common product catalog and a customized assortment for each customer type.

A configuration 𝑨=(A1,…,AK)\boldsymbol{A}=(A_{1},\ldots,A_{K}) specifies an assortment AkA_{k} for each type kk. Its common product catalog is I𝑨=⋃k=1KAkI_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}A_{k}. Define the set of feasible configurations by

𝔄B={𝑨=(A1,…,AK):Ak⊆𝒩∀k,|⋃k=1KAk|≤B}.\mathfrak{A}_{B}=\left\{\boldsymbol{A}=(A_{1},\ldots,A_{K}):A_{k}\subseteq\mathcal{N}\ \forall k,\quad\left|\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}A_{k}\right|\leq B\right\}.

The common-catalog constraint is important: although different customer types may be offered different assortments, they share the same initial inventory, and a product may be purchased by several types.

Let τk\tau_{k} denote the expected number of type-kk arrivals. For any modified reward vector 𝝆∈ℚn\boldsymbol{\rho}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n}, define the joint assortment and customization (JAC) problem as

JACB⁡(𝝆)=max⁡∑k=1K𝑨∈𝔄B⁡τk​∑i∈Akρi​πk​(i,Ak).\operatorname{JAC}_{B}(\boldsymbol{\rho})=\max_{\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathfrak{A}_{B}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tau_{k}\sum_{i\in A_{k}}\rho_{i}\pi^{k}(i,A_{k}). (2)

We assume that this problem admits an αJAC\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}-approximation in polynomial time for every rational reward vector.

Main result.

Our DAP results are obtained by extending the fluid relaxation and inventory construction developed for SA to configurations of personalized assortments. The resulting algorithms have a particularly simple operating structure. They select both the initial inventory and one assortment AkA_{k} for each customer type before the selling horizon begins. Whenever a type-kk customer arrives, the DM offers every product in AkA_{k} that remains in stock. Thus, the assortment offered to each type changes only through stockouts, and the DM never strategically removes an available product or reoptimizes assortments during the selling horizon.

Despite this restriction, our performance guarantees are measured against the optimal DAP policy, which may dynamically adapt assortments to customer types, remaining inventory, and purchase history.

Theorem 2.3 (Approximation for DAP)

Suppose Assumption 2.1 holds for every customer type and that (2) admits a polynomial-time αJAC\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}-approximation for every rational reward vector. Then there exists a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that selects an initial inventory vector 𝐜^∈𝒞B\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}\in\mathcal{C}_{B} almost surely and a fixed assortment AkA_{k} for each customer type kk, such that offering AkA_{k} intersected with the in-stock products to every type-kk customer achieves the following guarantees:

  1. (i)

    If TT is deterministic or Poisson distributed, the expected revenue is at least 0.486​αJAC​OPTDAP0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}.

  2. (ii)

    If TT is IFR distributed, the expected revenue is at least 0.4328​αJAC​OPTDAP0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}.

Theorem 2.3 shows that a substantial guaranteed fraction of the optimal adaptive DAP revenue can be obtained through a type-specific show-all policy, provided that the initial inventory and type-specific assortments are selected jointly. In particular, no dynamic assortment reoptimization is required after the selling horizon begins. This illustrates how coordinating initial inventory and customer-specific assortment decisions can reduce the need for more sophisticated dynamic assortment control.

For MNL choice, a polynomial-time approximation algorithm for JAC achieves a factor arbitrarily close to 1/21/2. Consequently, Theorem 2.3 yields DAP guarantees approaching 0.2430.243 for deterministic or Poisson arrivals and 0.21640.2164 for IFR arrivals. More generally, any improvement in the approximation factor for JAC translates directly into an improved DAP guarantee through our framework.

3 Proof of Theorem 2.1

The proof of Theorem 2.1 proceeds in three main steps, which we summarize below. All proofs from this section can be found in Appendix A.

Step 1: A fluid upper bound (Section 3.1).

We begin by introducing a fluid linear programming relaxation that allocates the expected customer arrivals across assortments, subject to constraints on total expected sales and the cardinality of each assortment. At this stage, we do not require an integral inventory decision; the relaxation accounts only for the expected consumption of inventory. We establish that every feasible inventory vector induces a feasible fluid solution with the same expected revenue, and hence the optimal fluid objective upper-bounds OPTSA\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}. Following Fu et al. (2026), we solve this relaxation through its dual, whose constraints are indexed by assortments. Separating these constraints amounts to solving a cardinality-constrained assortment optimization problem with modified product revenues. Thus, our tractability assumption provides a separation oracle for generating violated dual constraints and solving the fluid LP in polynomial time. Moreover, since the fluid LP has only two resource constraints, we can select an optimal basic solution supported on at most two assortments.

Step 2: Constructing fractional inventory (Section 3.2).

For each assortment SS in the support of the optimal fluid solution, we construct a fractional inventory vector that stocks only products in SS. We continue to set aside integrality in this step, while requiring that the total inventory does not exceed BB. The construction balances the inventory needed to stock a product against the inventory needed to serve its expected demand. To evaluate the resulting allocation, we introduce a separable expected-revenue lower bound based on the demand generated by offering SS throughout the horizon. Substitutability connects this auxiliary demand model to the show-all process, while bounds on expected truncated demand guide the choice of fractional inventory.

Let DSD_{S} and VSV_{S} denote, respectively, the expected total demand and revenue from offering SS throughout the horizon without inventory constraints, and write dS=DS/Bd_{S}=D_{S}/B. We show that the fractional inventory vector has an associated revenue lower bound of at least LS=VS/(C+dS)L_{S}=V_{S}/(C+d_{S}), where C≈1.057C\approx 1.057. We then select the assortment with the largest value of LSL_{S}. The two constraints in the fluid LP imply that this certificate is at least a 1/(1+C)≈0.4861/(1+C)\approx 0.486 fraction of the optimal fluid objective. Thus, this step identifies a capacity-feasible fractional inventory vector with the desired performance certificate, leaving only its conversion into an integral stocking decision.

Step 3: Randomized rounding (Section 3.3).

Finally, we convert the selected fractional inventory vector into an integral one using the dependent-rounding procedure of Gandhi et al. (2006). Applied to the fractional parts of the inventory levels, with a dummy coordinate accounting for unused capacity, this procedure rounds each coordinate to its floor or ceiling, preserves its expectation, and satisfies the total inventory constraint in every realization. The key observation is that the expected truncated-demand function is affine between consecutive integer inventory levels, because customer demand is integer-valued. Consequently, the rounding preserves the expected value of the separable revenue lower bound from Step 2. Since this lower bound is dominated by the expected show-all revenue for every realized integral inventory vector, the rounded solution retains the certificate LSL_{S} in expectation. Combining the three steps therefore yields a 1/(1+C)1/(1+C)-approximation without requiring any assortment decisions after the initial inventory is selected.

3.1 Step 1: A fluid upper bound

We begin with the fluid relaxation of Fu et al. (2026), which allocates the expected customer arrivals across assortments while accounting for the total inventory capacity in expectation. At this stage, we do not select an inventory vector or impose integrality on expected sales. Instead, the relaxation retains two implications of the inventory constraint: the expected number of units sold cannot exceed BB, and every offered assortment contains at most BB products. We first establish that the resulting linear program upper-bounds OPTSA\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}} and then describe how to solve it using a cardinality-constrained assortment optimization oracle.

The fluid relaxation.

Let τ=𝔼⁡[T]\tau={\mathbb{E}}[T] denote the expected number of customer arrivals, and define 𝒮B={S⊆𝒩:|S|≤B}\mathcal{S}_{B}=\{S\subseteq\mathcal{N}:|S|\leq B\}. We assume τ>0\tau>0, since the problem is trivial otherwise. For every assortment S∈𝒮BS\in\mathcal{S}_{B}, let

μiS=τ​π​(i,S),DS=∑i∈SμiS,VS=∑i∈Sri​μiS.\mu_{i}^{S}=\tau\pi(i,S),\qquad D_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\mu_{i}^{S},\qquad V_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}\mu_{i}^{S}.

Thus, μiS\mu_{i}^{S} is the expected demand for product ii if assortment SS is offered to every arriving customer without inventory restrictions, while DSD_{S} and VSV_{S} are the corresponding expected total demand and revenue. For each S∈𝒮BS\in\mathcal{S}_{B}, introduce a nonnegative variable fSf_{S}, representing the expected number of customers offered SS, normalized by τ\tau. The fluid relaxation is

OPTFL=max𝒇≥𝟎\displaystyle\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}=\max_{\boldsymbol{f}\geq\boldsymbol{0}} ∑S∈𝒮BfS​VS\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{B}}f_{S}V_{S} (FLUID-LP)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑S∈𝒮BfS​DS≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{B}}f_{S}D_{S}\leq B,
∑S∈𝒮BfS≤1.\displaystyle\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{B}}f_{S}\leq 1.

The first constraint limits total expected sales, while the second limits the expected number of customers allocated to assortments. Unlike the original problem, (FLUID-LP) does not require the assortment allocations to arise from an integral starting inventory vector or a stockout-driven sequence of offered assortments. By Proposition 1 of Fu et al. (2026), its optimal value satisfies OPTFL≥OPTSA\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}. This upper-bound property holds for arbitrary choice models and any arrival count with finite mean that is independent of customer preferences; substitutability and the distributional assumptions on TT enter our subsequent inventory construction.

Solving the fluid relaxation.

We also follow Fu et al. (2026) to solve (FLUID-LP). Although the primal has exponentially many assortment variables, its dual has only two nonnegative variables, λ\lambda and η\eta, associated with the expected-sales and customer-allocation constraints, respectively. The dual constraints are η+λ​DS≥VS\eta+\lambda D_{S}\geq V_{S} for every S∈𝒮BS\in\mathcal{S}_{B}. Separating these constraints requires solving

maxS∈𝒮B⁡{VS−λ​DS}=τ​maxS⊆𝒩|S|≤B​∑i∈S(ri−λ)⋅π⁡(i,S).\max_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{B}}\{V_{S}-\lambda D_{S}\}=\tau\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}S\subseteq\mathcal{N}\\ |S|\leq B\end{subarray}}\sum_{i\in S}(r_{i}-\lambda)\cdot\pi(i,S).

Thus, a cardinality-constrained assortment optimization oracle with modified rewards ρi=ri−λ\rho_{i}=r_{i}-\lambda identifies a violated dual constraint whenever the displayed value exceeds η\eta, and otherwise certifies feasibility. This provides a separation oracle for dual constraint generation. Under our computational assumptions, Proposition 6 of Fu et al. (2026) establishes polynomial-time solvability of the fluid LP through the ellipsoid method.

An optimal solution with small support.

Since (FLUID-LP) has only two resource constraints, it admits an optimal basic solution supported on at most two assortments, as noted in Section 4.1 of Fu et al. (2026). Fix such a solution 𝒇⋆\boldsymbol{f}^{\star}, and let 𝒮⋆={S∈𝒮B:fS⋆>0}\mathcal{S}^{\star}=\{S\in\mathcal{S}_{B}:f_{S}^{\star}>0\} denote its support. Then |𝒮⋆|≤2|\mathcal{S}^{\star}|\leq 2 and

∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆​VS=OPTFL,∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆​DS≤B,∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆≤1.\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}V_{S}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}},\qquad\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}D_{S}\leq B,\qquad\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}\leq 1.

In the next step, we construct a capacity-feasible fractional inventory vector for each S∈𝒮⋆S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star} and use these inequalities to compare the strongest resulting revenue certificate with OPTFL\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}.

Computational complexity.

Step 1 obtains an optimal fluid solution with at most two supporting assortments in polynomial time under our static assortment optimization assumption. Step 2 evaluates the choice probabilities for these assortments and constructs their fractional inventory vectors using rational arithmetic. Finally, the rounding operates only on the fractional parts of the inventory coordinates and requires O⁡(n)O(n) pairwise updates; it does not enumerate the individual inventory units. Exact sampling of the rational update probabilities can be implemented in expected polynomial time. Thus, the complete algorithm has expected running time polynomial in the input encoding.

3.4 A Factor-Two Gap for the Fluid Relaxation

Before proceeding, we show that the fluid relaxation (FLUID-LP) can overestimate the optimal expected revenue by a factor approaching two. Thus, no algorithm whose performance is measured directly relative to OPTFL\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}} can obtain a uniform approximation guarantee strictly larger than 1/21/2. The example holds even under the standard MNL choice model with only two products and a deterministic number of customer arrivals.

Proposition 3.4

There exists a sequence of MNL instances for which

OPTSAOPTFL⟶12.\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}}\longrightarrow\frac{1}{2}.

Proposition 3.4 implies that the factor 1/21/2 is a fundamental upper bound on any uniform performance guarantee measured directly against OPTFL\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}. In particular, improving our 0.4860.486 guarantee all the way to 1/21/2 would be essentially tight relative to this relaxation.

4 Proof of Theorem 2.2

We now establish the approximation guarantee for IFR-distributed customer arrivals. Our approach follows the same three steps as the proof of Theorem 2.1, with two modifications to the fractional inventory construction. First, we replace the Poisson truncated-demand lower bound with one based on a geometric distribution. Second, we introduce separate coefficients for the two constraints of the fluid LP, allowing us to obtain a stronger approximation guarantee.

Step 1: A fluid upper bound (Section 4.1).

We use the same fluid relaxation (FLUID-LP) introduced in Section 3.1. Its upper-bound property holds for any distribution of TT with finite mean, including IFR distributions, and its solution requires only the cardinality- constrained assortment optimization oracle. As before, we fix an optimal basic solution supported on at most two assortments.

Step 2: Constructing fractional inventory (Section 4.2).

For each supporting assortment SS, we construct a fractional inventory vector supported on SS and associate it with a separable revenue lower bound. The main difference is that hypothetical product demand under IFR arrivals need not be dominated in convex order by a Poisson random variable with the same mean. Instead, we show that it is dominated by a geometric random variable, which provides a lower bound on expected truncated sales. Using this comparison, we develop a new inventory allocation and obtain a certificate of the form

LSIFR=VSC0+C1​DS/B,L_{S}^{\mathrm{IFR}}=\frac{V_{S}}{C_{0}+C_{1}D_{S}/B},

where C0=1.2148C_{0}=1.2148 and C1=1.0955C_{1}=1.0955. We select the supporting assortment with the largest certificate and show that its value is at least 1/(C0+C1)>0.43281/(C_{0}+C_{1})>0.4328 times the optimal fluid objective.

Step 3: Randomized rounding (Section 4.3).

Finally, we apply the same dependent-rounding procedure as in Section 3.3. Since geometric demand is integer-valued, its expected truncated-demand function is affine between consecutive integer inventory levels. Thus, the rounding preserves our new revenue surrogate in expectation, while satisfying the capacity constraint almost surely. Combining the three steps establishes Theorem 2.2.

4.1 Step 1: A fluid upper bound

We continue to use the fluid relaxation (FLUID-LP), which depends on the arrival distribution only through its mean τ=𝔼⁡[T]\tau={\mathbb{E}}[T]. Recall that, for each S∈𝒮BS\in\mathcal{S}_{B}, we define

μiS=τ​π​(i,S),DS=∑i∈SμiS,VS=∑i∈Sri​μiS.\mu_{i}^{S}=\tau\pi(i,S),\qquad D_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}\mu_{i}^{S},\qquad V_{S}=\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}\mu_{i}^{S}.

As discussed in Section 3.1, the upper-bound property OPTFL≥OPTSA\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}} holds for arbitrary distributions of TT with finite mean.

Moreover, the same assortment optimization oracle allows us to solve the fluid LP in polynomial time. Fix an optimal basic solution 𝒇⋆\boldsymbol{f}^{\star} with support 𝒮⋆\mathcal{S}^{\star}, where |𝒮⋆|≤2|\mathcal{S}^{\star}|\leq 2 and

∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆​VS=OPTFL,∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆​DS≤B,∑S∈𝒮⋆fS⋆≤1.\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}V_{S}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}},\qquad\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}D_{S}\leq B,\qquad\sum_{S\in\mathcal{S}^{\star}}f_{S}^{\star}\leq 1.

The remainder of the proof is devoted to constructing an inventory vector whose expected revenue captures a constant fraction of this fluid objective.

4.2 Step 2: Constructing fractional inventory

As in Section 3.2, we construct a fractional inventory vector for each assortment in 𝒮⋆\mathcal{S}^{\star}. We first establish the geometric-demand comparison that replaces the Poisson lower bound used previously.

A geometric revenue surrogate.

For μ>0\mu>0, let GμG_{\mu} denote a geometric random variable on ℤ+\mathbb{Z}_{+} with mean μ\mu, so that

Pr⁡(Gμ=k)=11+μ​(μ1+μ)k,k∈ℤ+.\Pr(G_{\mu}=k)=\frac{1}{1+\mu}\left(\frac{\mu}{1+\mu}\right)^{k},\qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

The new ingredient is that a binomial random variable with an IFR-distributed number of trials is dominated in convex order by a geometric random variable with the same mean. The rounding procedure is identical to that in Section 3.3. Fix the selected assortment S^\widehat{S} and fractional inventory vector 𝒛=𝒛S^\boldsymbol{z}=\boldsymbol{z}^{\widehat{S}}. Computational complexity.

Step 1 uses the same polynomial-time fluid optimization procedure as Section 3.1. Step 2 evaluates the demand parameters and constructs fractional inventory using rational arithmetic, since C0C_{0} and C1C_{1} are fixed rational constants. Finally, Lemma 4.3 establishes that the admissibility condition also holds for C0⋆,C1⋆C_{0}^{\star},C_{1}^{\star}, whose sum equals 1/(1−w)1/(1-w). 4.4 Tightness Relative to the Fluid Relaxation

We conclude by showing that the IFR approximation factor is essentially tight relative to the fluid relaxation. Specifically, we construct a sequence of instances for which the optimal expected show-all revenue approaches only a (1−w)(1-w)-fraction of OPTFL\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}. The example uses geometric arrivals and independent product requests without substitution, demonstrating that this gap does not require complicated choice behavior.

Proposition 4.4

There exists a sequence of instances with IFR-distributed arrival counts and substitutable choice probabilities for which

OPTSAOPTFL⟶1−w,\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}}\longrightarrow 1-w,

where w∈(0,1)w\in(0,1) is the unique solution to w​ew=1we^{w}=1.

The proof is provided in Appendix A. In the constructed instances, the fluid relaxation obtains substantial revenue from both a high-demand product and many products with vanishingly small expected demand. An integral inventory decision, however, must reserve at least one unit for each stocked low-demand product, thereby reducing the capacity available to the high-demand product. The resulting gap is amplified by the variability of geometric demand.

Proposition 4.4, together with Theorem 2.2, establishes that 1−w≈0.43285671-w\approx 0.4328567 is the sharp uniform comparison factor for this fluid relaxation under IFR arrivals. Consequently, our 0.43280.4328 approximation guarantee is essentially tight relative to the fluid benchmark.

5 Proof of Theorem 2.3

We now extend the preceding analysis to dynamic assortment personalization. The proof follows the same three steps as the SA analysis, replacing individual assortments with configurations of type-specific assortments that share a common product catalog. The main additional ingredients are a configuration-based fluid upper bound and a revenue comparison for personalized assortment plans. Once these are established, the fractional inventory constructions and rounding arguments developed for SA apply without modification.

Step 1: A configuration-based fluid upper bound (Section 5.1).

We formulate a fluid relaxation whose columns are configurations 𝑨=(A1,…,AK)\boldsymbol{A}=(A_{1},\ldots,A_{K}) satisfying |⋃kAk|≤B|\bigcup_{k}A_{k}|\leq B. We show that every feasible initial inventory and adaptive personalized policy induces a feasible fluid solution with the same expected revenue. The common-catalog constraint is essential: different types may receive different assortments, but these assortments must draw from products that can be stocked together. An αJAC\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}-approximation for the joint assortment and customization problem yields a feasible fluid solution with a corresponding approximation guarantee, supported on at most two configurations.

Step 2: Constructing fractional inventory (Section 5.2).

For each supporting configuration, we construct an inventory vector supported on its common catalog. Hypothetical demand aggregates purchases across all customer types, allowing the same inventory to serve multiple types. Under deterministic or Poisson arrivals, we apply the Poisson inventory bound from Section 3.2; under IFR arrivals, we use the geometric inventory bound from Section 4.2. These constructions give configuration-level revenue certificates of the same form as in the SA analysis. We select the configuration with the largest certificate.

Step 3: Randomized rounding and implementation (Section 5.3).

We apply the dependent-rounding procedure from Section 3.3 to the selected fractional inventory. The implemented policy fixes one planned assortment for each customer type before the selling horizon begins and subsequently offers every in-stock product from that assortment. The same interpolation argument preserves the revenue certificate in expectation. Thus, the policy requires no dynamic assortment reoptimization, although its guarantee is measured against the optimal fully adaptive DAP policy.

All new lemma proofs are provided in Appendix A.

5.1 Step 1: A configuration-based fluid upper bound

Recall that 𝔄B\mathfrak{A}_{B} denotes the collection of feasible configurations defined in Section 2.3. For 𝑨=(A1,…,AK)∈𝔄B\boldsymbol{A}=(A_{1},\ldots,A_{K})\in\mathfrak{A}_{B}, its common catalog is I𝑨=⋃k=1KAkI_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}A_{k}, with |I𝑨|≤B|I_{\boldsymbol{A}}|\leq B.

Let τk\tau_{k} denote the expected number of type-kk arrivals. Thus, τk=∑t=1Tλk​t\tau_{k}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\lambda_{kt} when TT is deterministic, and τk=τ​λk\tau_{k}=\tau\lambda_{k} when TT is random and customer types are independent and identically distributed. For every configuration 𝑨\boldsymbol{A}, define

μi𝑨=∑k=1Kτk​πk​(i,Ak),D𝑨=∑i∈𝒩μi𝑨,V𝑨=∑i∈𝒩ri​μi𝑨.\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\tau_{k}\pi^{k}(i,A_{k}),\qquad D_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}}\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}},\qquad V_{\boldsymbol{A}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{N}}r_{i}\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}.

These quantities describe the expected product-level demand, total demand, and revenue when each type-kk customer is offered AkA_{k} without inventory restrictions.

s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑𝑨∈𝔄Bf𝑨​D𝑨≤B,\displaystyle\sum_{\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathfrak{A}_{B}}f_{\boldsymbol{A}}D_{\boldsymbol{A}}\leq B,

The formulation has the same two-constraint structure as (FLUID-LP). Its columns, however, specify a complete personalized assortment plan rather than a single assortment.

Lemma 5.1 (Configuration fluid upper bound)

The optimal value of (FLUID-DAP) satisfies Uconf≥OPTDAPU_{\mathrm{conf}}\geq\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}.

To establish the lemma, we fix an initial inventory and an adaptive policy, and record the distribution of assortments offered to each customer type. These distributions can be combined into a distribution over configurations supported on the initial product catalog. The resulting fluid solution preserves the policy’s expected sales and revenue. In particular, this construction does not partition physical inventory across customer types.

For λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, define

H⁡(λ)=max𝑨∈𝔄B⁡{V𝑨−λ​D𝑨}.H(\lambda)=\max_{\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathfrak{A}_{B}}\{V_{\boldsymbol{A}}-\lambda D_{\boldsymbol{A}}\}.

Thus, the assumed JAC oracle gives an αJAC\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}-approximation to the Lagrangian subproblem for every capacity price λ\lambda.

For every ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), a feasible solution to (FLUID-DAP) with objective value F≥αJAC​(1−ε)​UconfF\geq\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}(1-\varepsilon)U_{\mathrm{conf}} can be computed in time polynomial in the input encoding and log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon). The returned solution is supported on at most two configurations.

The proof uses a bisection search over the capacity price. We retain one configuration whose expected demand exceeds BB and another whose expected demand is at most BB. Mixing these configurations to meet the capacity constraint gives the desired approximation. This argument does not require the approximate oracle’s output to vary monotonically with the capacity price.

Fix the solution 𝒇\boldsymbol{f} returned by Lemma 5.2, and let 𝔄+={𝑨:f𝑨>0,D𝑨>0}\mathfrak{A}^{+}=\{\boldsymbol{A}:f_{\boldsymbol{A}}>0,\,D_{\boldsymbol{A}}>0\}. Configurations with zero demand also have zero revenue and can be discarded without changing FF or renormalizing the remaining weights. If F=0F=0, then OPTDAP=0\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}=0, and the result is immediate. Henceforth, assume F>0F>0.

The proof applies substitutability separately to each customer type. The demand comparisons from the SA analysis therefore remain applicable after aggregating across types.

≤L𝑨^​(κ0​∑𝑨∈𝔄+f𝑨+κ1B​∑𝑨∈𝔄+f𝑨​D𝑨)\displaystyle\leq L_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}\left(\kappa_{0}\sum_{\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathfrak{A}^{+}}f_{\boldsymbol{A}}+\frac{\kappa_{1}}{B}\sum_{\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathfrak{A}^{+}}f_{\boldsymbol{A}}D_{\boldsymbol{A}}\right)
≤(κ0+κ1)​L𝑨^.\displaystyle\leq(\kappa_{0}+\kappa_{1})L_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}.

Therefore, the selected fractional inventory satisfies

ℛ𝑨^​(𝒛𝑨^)≥L𝑨^≥Fκ0+κ1.\mathcal{R}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}})\geq L_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}\geq\frac{F}{\kappa_{0}+\kappa_{1}}.

5.3 Step 3: Randomized rounding and implementation

Apply the dependent-rounding procedure from Section 3.3 to 𝒛𝑨^\boldsymbol{z}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}, independently of future customer arrivals and preferences. Let 𝒄^​(ω)\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega) denote the resulting integral inventory vector. The same rounding properties ensure that it is supported on I𝑨^I_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}} and belongs to 𝒞B\mathcal{C}_{B} almost surely.

Both gμg_{\mu} and gμGg_{\mu}^{\mathrm{G}} are affine between consecutive integers. Hence, the argument in Lemma 3.3 applies to the configuration surrogate and gives

𝔼ω​[ℛ𝑨^​(𝒄^​(ω))]=ℛ𝑨^​(𝒛𝑨^).\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega))\right]=\mathcal{R}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}).

Set σ^=σ𝑨^\widehat{\sigma}=\sigma^{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}. The algorithm implements this policy throughout the selling horizon: when type kk arrives, it offers A^k\widehat{A}_{k} intersected with the current in-stock set. The fluid mixture is used only to identify the selected configuration; it is not sampled anew during the selling horizon.

Completing the approximation guarantee.

Using Lemma 5.3, (13), (14), and Lemma 5.2, we obtain

𝔼ω​[RevDAP​(𝒄^​(ω),σ^)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathrm{Rev}^{\mathrm{DAP}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega),\widehat{\sigma})\right] ≥𝔼ω​[ℛ𝑨^​(𝒄^​(ω))]\displaystyle\geq\mathbb{E}_{\omega}\left[\mathcal{R}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol{c}}(\omega))\right]
=ℛ𝑨^​(𝒛𝑨^)\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}(\boldsymbol{z}^{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}})
≥L𝑨^\displaystyle\geq L_{\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}}
≥Fκ0+κ1\displaystyle\geq\frac{F}{\kappa_{0}+\kappa_{1}}
≥αJAC​(1−ε)κ0+κ1​Uconf\displaystyle\geq\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}(1-\varepsilon)}{\kappa_{0}+\kappa_{1}}U_{\mathrm{conf}}
≥αJAC​(1−ε)κ0+κ1​OPTDAP.\displaystyle\geq\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}}(1-\varepsilon)}{\kappa_{0}+\kappa_{1}}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{DAP}}.

The revenue function already averages over customer arrivals, types, and purchase decisions; the outer expectation concerns only the initial rounding randomness.

Taking ε=10−4\varepsilon=10^{-4} gives

1−ε1+C=999920574>0.486,1−εC0+C1=999923103>0.4328.\frac{1-\varepsilon}{1+C}=\frac{9999}{20574}>0.486,\qquad\frac{1-\varepsilon}{C_{0}+C_{1}}=\frac{9999}{23103}>0.4328.

Consequently, the algorithm achieves the stated guarantees of 0.486​αJAC0.486\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for deterministic or Poisson arrivals and 0.4328​αJAC0.4328\alpha_{\mathrm{JAC}} for IFR arrivals.

Computational complexity and policy structure.

Lemma 5.2 computes a fluid solution with at most two supporting configurations using polynomially many calls to the JAC oracle. The candidate inventories and certificates are evaluated using rational arithmetic, and rounding has the same expected polynomial running time as in Section 3.3. During the selling horizon, the policy merely identifies the arriving type and removes unavailable products from its predetermined assortment.

In particular, the policy never strategically withholds an available product from its planned assortment, introduces a previously excluded product following a stockout, or resolves an assortment optimization problem during the horizon. Nevertheless, its performance is compared with the optimal adaptive DAP policy. This completes the proof of Theorem 2.3.

Appendix A Proof from Section 3

A.1 Proof of Lemma 3.1

Consider the hypothetical demand generated by offering SS to every customer, irrespective of inventory availability. Let YiSY_{i}^{S} denote the number of customers who select product ii in this hypothetical process. Conditional on TT, its marginal distribution is Binomial⁡(T,π⁡(i,S))\operatorname{Binomial}(T,\pi(i,S)).

Under the actual show-all process, every offered assortment is a subset of SS. Whenever product ii remains available, substitutability implies that its purchase probability is at least π⁡(i,S)\pi(i,S). A productwise coupling therefore gives

Rev⁡(𝒄)≥∑i∈Sri​𝔼​[min⁡{ci,YiS}].\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{c})\geq\sum_{i\in S}r_{i}{\mathbb{E}}[\min\{c_{i},Y_{i}^{S}\}]. (15)

This is the fixed-assortment revenue comparison discussed in Remark 2 and the proof of Proposition 2 of Fu et al. (2026).

When TT is Poisson distributed, thinning gives YiS∼Poisson⁡(μiS)Y_{i}^{S}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\mu_{i}^{S}), and the result follows directly. When TT is deterministic, YiSY_{i}^{S} is binomial with mean μiS\mu_{i}^{S}. A binomial random variable is dominated in convex order by a Poisson random variable with the same mean. Since x↦min⁡{ci,x}x\mapsto\min\{c_{i},x\} is concave, it follows that

𝔼⁡[min⁡{ci,YiS}]≥𝔼⁡[min⁡{ci,XμiS}]=gμiS​(ci).{\mathbb{E}}[\min\{c_{i},Y_{i}^{S}\}]\geq{\mathbb{E}}[\min\{c_{i},X_{\mu_{i}^{S}}\}]=g_{\mu_{i}^{S}}(c_{i}).

For completeness, the convex-order comparison can be established by replacing the independent Bernoulli summands one at a time by independent Poisson variables with the same means. For any concave function φ\varphi and nonnegative integer kk, φ⁡(k)≤φ⁡(0)+k⁡(φ⁡(1)−φ⁡(0))\varphi(k)\leq\varphi(0)+k(\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)). Thus, among nonnegative integer-valued random variables of mean p∈[0,1]p\in[0,1], a Bernoulli random variable maximizes the expectation of φ\varphi. Conditioning on the other summands and applying this observation successively proves the required comparison. Combining it with (15) completes the proof.

Fix an integer m≥2m\geq 2. Consider an instance with two products, inventory capacity B=1B=1, and a deterministic number T=mT=m of customer arrivals. Customer choice follows an MNL model with outside-option weight w0=1w_{0}=1 and product weights

w1=1m2−1,w2=m.w_{1}=\frac{1}{m^{2}-1},\qquad w_{2}=m.

The product revenues are

r1=m,r2=1.r_{1}=m,\qquad r_{2}=1.

The singleton purchase probabilities are therefore

π⁡(1,{1})=w11+w1=1m2,π⁡(2,{2})=w21+w2=mm+1.\pi(1,\{1\})=\frac{w_{1}}{1+w_{1}}=\frac{1}{m^{2}},\qquad\pi(2,\{2\})=\frac{w_{2}}{1+w_{2}}=\frac{m}{m+1}.

We first characterize the optimal inventory decision. Since B=1B=1, the DM can stock at most one unit of one product. If product 11 is stocked, it generates revenue mm if at least one of the mm customers purchases it. Hence,

Rev⁡(𝒆1)=m⁡[1−(1−1m2)m]≤1,\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{e}_{1})=m\left[1-\left(1-\frac{1}{m^{2}}\right)^{m}\right]\leq 1,

Rev⁡(𝒆1)⟶1.\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{e}_{1})\longrightarrow 1.

OPTSA=max⁡{Rev⁡(𝒆1),Rev⁡(𝒆2)}⟶1.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}=\max\{\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{e}_{1}),\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{e}_{2})\}\longrightarrow 1. (19)

f{2}​D2⟶1andf{1}⟶1.f_{\{2\}}D_{2}\longrightarrow 1\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_{\{1\}}\longrightarrow 1.

lim infm→∞OPTFL≥2.\liminf_{m\rightarrow\infty}\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}\geq 2.

Fix an assortment SS and an integral inventory vector 𝒄\boldsymbol{c} supported on SS. Let XiSX_{i}^{S} denote hypothetical demand for product ii when SS is offered to every customer without inventory restrictions. As in the proof of Lemma 3.1, substitutability gives

We first show that any nonnegative integer-valued IFR random variable TT with mean τ\tau satisfies T≤cxGτT\leq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_{\tau}. Let sk=Pr⁡(T≥k)s_{k}=\Pr(T\geq k). H⁡(k)≤τ1+τ​H​(k−1).H(k)\leq\frac{\tau}{1+\tau}H(k-1).

for all integers k≥0k\geq 0. The comparison extends to all real thresholds by linear interpolation, since both random variables are integer-valued. As they have the same mean, the stop-loss characterization of convex order yields T≤cxGτT\leq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_{\tau}.

B.4 Proof of Proposition 4.4

For each integer B≥2B\geq 2, consider BB products consisting of one product hh and B−1B-1 additional products. Let εB=B−2\varepsilon_{B}=B^{-2} and aB=⌊w​B⌋/Ba_{B}=\lfloor wB\rfloor/B, so that aB→wa_{B}\to w. The number of arriving customers is geometric on ℤ+\mathbb{Z}_{+} with mean BB, which is an IFR distribution.

Define the full-horizon demand means by

μh=B−(B−1)εB,μi=εB(i≠h).\mu_{h}=B-(B-1)\varepsilon_{B},\qquad\mu_{i}=\varepsilon_{B}\quad(i\neq h).

Each customer independently requests product ii with probability pi=μi/Bp_{i}=\mu_{i}/B, and purchases it if it is available. Otherwise, the customer leaves without purchasing. Since ∑ipi=1\sum_{i}p_{i}=1, this defines a valid choice model with

π(i,S)=pi𝟏{i∈S}.\pi(i,S)=p_{i}\mathbf{1}\{i\in S\}.

It satisfies substitutability. Set the product revenues to

rh=1,ri=aBεB(i≠h).r_{h}=1,\qquad r_{i}=\frac{a_{B}}{\varepsilon_{B}}\quad(i\neq h).

The fluid optimum.

Offering the full assortment throughout the horizon generates expected total demand exactly BB, so assigning it fluid weight one is feasible. Moreover, removing a product does not increase demand for any other product. Therefore, the full assortment maximizes unlimited-inventory expected revenue, and

OPTFL=μh+(B−1)​aB.\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}=\mu_{h}+(B-1)a_{B}. (23)

Consequently,

OPTFLB⟶1+w.\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}}{B}\longrightarrow 1+w.

An upper bound on the optimal inventory revenue.

Consider any feasible integral inventory vector, and let k∈{0,…,B}k\in\{0,\ldots,B\} denote the inventory of product hh. Bernoulli thinning of the geometric arrival count implies that hypothetical demand for hh is geometric with mean μh\mu_{h}. Its expected sales therefore equal

μh​[1−(μh1+μh)k].\mu_{h}\left[1-\left(\frac{\mu_{h}}{1+\mu_{h}}\right)^{k}\right].

Every stocked product i≠hi\neq h generates expected revenue at most its unlimited-inventory expected revenue ri​μi=aBr_{i}\mu_{i}=a_{B}. Since at most B−kB-k such products can be stocked,

Rev⁡(𝒄)≤μh​[1−(μh1+μh)k]+aB​(B−k).\mathrm{Rev}(\boldsymbol{c})\leq\mu_{h}\left[1-\left(\frac{\mu_{h}}{1+\mu_{h}}\right)^{k}\right]+a_{B}(B-k).

Writing x=k/Bx=k/B, the right-hand side divided by BB converges uniformly for x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] to

φ⁡(x)=1−e−x+w⁡(1−x).\varphi(x)=1-e^{-x}+w(1-x).

Indeed, μh/B→1\mu_{h}/B\to 1 and B​log⁡(μh/(1+μh))→−1B\log(\mu_{h}/(1+\mu_{h}))\to-1. Since φ′​(x)=e−x−w\varphi^{\prime}(x)=e^{-x}-w, the maximum is attained at x=−log⁡w=wx=-\log w=w, with value

φ⁡(w)=1−w2.\varphi(w)=1-w^{2}.

It follows that

lim supB→∞OPTSAB≤1−w2.\limsup_{B\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{B}\leq 1-w^{2}.

Matching lower bound.

Now stock kB=⌊w​B⌋k_{B}=\lfloor wB\rfloor units of product hh and one unit of each of B−kBB-k_{B} additional products. Each stocked product i≠hi\neq h generates expected revenue

ri​Pr⁡(GεB≥1)=aB1+εB.r_{i}\Pr(G_{\varepsilon_{B}}\geq 1)=\frac{a_{B}}{1+\varepsilon_{B}}.

The resulting total expected revenue divided by BB converges to

1−e−w+w⁡(1−w)=1−w2,1-e^{-w}+w(1-w)=1-w^{2},

where we use e−w=we^{-w}=w. Therefore,

OPTSAB⟶1−w2.\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{B}\longrightarrow 1-w^{2}.

Combining this with (23), we obtain

OPTSAOPTFL⟶1−w21+w=1−w,\frac{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{SA}}}{\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{FL}}}\longrightarrow\frac{1-w^{2}}{1+w}=1-w,

Then ∑t=1TYi​t\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_{it} has the same distribution as Xi𝑨X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}.

We couple the actual process to these variables as follows. Given the history and type KtK_{t}, the actual assortment is St=AKt∩{j:cj,t>0}S_{t}=A_{K_{t}}\cap\{j:c_{j,t}>0\}. Write qi​t=πKt​(i,St)q_{it}=\pi^{K_{t}}(i,S_{t}). Use UtU_{t} to make the actual customer choose product ii exactly when Ut≤qi​tU_{t}\leq q_{it}. On the complementary event, use additional independent randomness to select among the other outcomes according to their conditional choice probabilities. This construction has the correct conditional choice distribution.

Whenever product ii remains in stock, substitutability implies qi​t≥pi​tq_{it}\geq p_{it}; if i∉AKti\notin A_{K_{t}}, both probabilities are zero. Therefore, a hypothetical request for ii is accompanied by an actual sale of ii whenever inventory of ii remains available. If Ni​(t)N_{i}(t) denotes cumulative actual sales through customer tt, induction gives

Ni​(t)≥min⁡{ci,∑s=1tYi​s}.N_{i}(t)\geq\min\left\{c_{i},\sum_{s=1}^{t}Y_{is}\right\}.

Evaluating at TT and taking expectations proves 𝔼⁡[Ni​(T)]≥𝔼⁡[min⁡{ci,Xi𝑨}]\mathbb{E}[N_{i}(T)]\geq\mathbb{E}[\min\{c_{i},X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\}]. The coupling is constructed separately for each product; a simultaneous coupling across products is unnecessary. Since revenues depend only on the purchased product, summing these expected-sales comparisons proves (25).

Deterministic and Poisson arrivals.

When TT is deterministic, the variables Yi​tY_{it} are independent across periods, with

Pr⁡(Yi​t=1)=∑k=1Kλk​t​πk​(i,Ak).\Pr(Y_{it}=1)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\lambda_{kt}\pi^{k}(i,A_{k}).

Thus, Xi𝑨X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}} is Poisson-binomial with mean μi𝑨\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}. The convex-order comparison used in the proof of Lemma 3.1 therefore gives

𝔼⁡[min⁡{ci,Xi𝑨}]≥gμi𝑨​(ci).\mathbb{E}[\min\{c_{i},X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\}]\geq g_{\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}}(c_{i}).

When TT is Poisson and types are independent and identically distributed, each hypothetical customer selects product ii with probability pi=∑kλk​πk​(i,Ak)p_{i}=\sum_{k}\lambda_{k}\pi^{k}(i,A_{k}). Poisson thinning gives Xi𝑨∼Poisson⁡(τ​pi)X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\tau p_{i}), where τ​pi=μi𝑨\tau p_{i}=\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}. The same comparison consequently holds with equality.

IFR arrivals.

When TT is IFR and types are independent and identically distributed, independently of TT, we have Xi𝑨|T∼Binomial⁡(T,pi)X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\mid T\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(T,p_{i}) with the same pip_{i}. The geometric convex-order argument in the proof of Lemma 4.1 gives Xi𝑨≤cxGμi𝑨X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\leq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_{\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}}. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[min⁡{ci,Xi𝑨}]≥gμi𝑨G​(ci).\mathbb{E}[\min\{c_{i},X_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}\}]\geq g_{\mu_{i}^{\boldsymbol{A}}}^{\mathrm{G}}(c_{i}).

Substituting the appropriate demand comparison into (25) proves the lemma in each arrival setting.
